screens.title: Variables, Constants, and Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Swift stores information and why those choices matter. We use named containers — variables and constants — to hold numbers, text, and true/false flags. Swift differentiates between mutable storage, declared with var, and immutable storage, declared with let. That distinction prevents accidental changes and makes reasoning about code easier. You will also meet the core types you use every day: Int for whole numbers, Double for decimals, String for text, and Bool for true/false values. Swift is type-safe and uses type inference to deduce types from initial values, while letting you add explicit type annotations when clarity or conversion is required. We will practice arithmetic operators and string interpolation to build readable output messages. Along the way, you’ll see common beginner mistakes — like trying to add strings and numbers without converting — and learn simple fixes. By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare variables and constants, pick appropriate types, use type inference with confidence, and produce formatted messages using interpolation. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you use every time you save or display data in an iOS app.

screens.title: var vs let — Mutability and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: Start by treating var and let as the language’s way of saying whether a named container is allowed to change. A variable declared with var is mutable: you may reassign it later. For example, you might declare a player's current score with var because it updates during gameplay. A constant declared with let is immutable; once set, its value cannot be changed. The compiler enforces this by producing an error if you attempt reassignment. That enforcement is important: prefer let whenever a value does not need to change. Using let makes reasoning and refactoring easier because other code can rely on that value staying stable. A common misconception is that var is always safer for flexibility; in fact, overusing var leads to accidental state changes and bugs. A short example: declare let maxAttempts = 3 for a fixed rule and var currentAttempt = 0 for a counter. Try reassigning maxAttempts and the compiler flags the error — that immediate feedback prevents runtime surprises. Takeaway: decide on mutability at the moment of declaration. Ask yourself, will this value need to change? If not, use let. That simple rule leads to cleaner, more reliable code.

keyIdea.title: Mutability rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer let for values that won’t change to reduce accidental modifications and make code easier to reason about.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › var vs let
Definition
var is used for values you will change; let is used for values that remain constant. The compiler enforces immutability for let.
Why it matters
  • Immutability reduces accidental changes and helps reasoning.
  • Compiler errors surface mistakes early during development.
  • Refactoring is safer when values are declared immutable by default.
Key Takeaway

Choose let when you know the value won’t change; use var sparingly for changing state like scores or counters.

Concrete Example
// Declaring a variable and a constant
var currentScore: Int = 0  // can change during the game
let maxAttempts: Int = 3   // fixed rule, never changes

// Changing a variable is allowed
currentScore = 150

// Reassigning a let causes a compile-time error
// maxAttempts = 4  // ERROR: Cannot assign to let constant
Misconception: using var everywhere is not safer. Immutability documents intent and prevents accidental bugs.

screens.title: Core Data Types: Int, Double, String, Bool
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the four foundational types in this chapter helps you model everyday app data. Int stores whole numbers like lives, scores, and counts. Use Int when fractional values are not needed. Double stores floating-point numbers with decimals — for example, a version number or a measured value. String holds text such as user names, messages, or labels. Bool represents true/false conditions and is ideal for flags like whether a game is paused. Picking the appropriate type makes operations clear: arithmetic on numbers, concatenation or interpolation on strings, and conditional checks on booleans. A common beginner error is treating numbers as strings for display and then attempting arithmetic without converting them back. Another frequent confusion is when to prefer Double over Int; if you need fractions or precise decimal math, choose Double. Remember that Swift is type-safe, so mixing types requires explicit conversion. For instance, to add a Double and an Int you convert the Int into a Double, or convert the Double to an Int if you accept truncation. These choices affect correctness and clarity. Think of types as labels that tell both the compiler and future readers what kind of data is expected and how it should be used.

screens.title: Int vs Double — Choosing numeric types
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between Int and Double depends on whether fractional values are meaningful in your domain. Use Int for counts, indices, and values that should remain whole, like the number of lives or integer scores. Use Double for measurements, averages, or version numbers that can include decimals. A common pitfall is mixing these types without conversion. For example, adding a Double to an Int directly is not allowed; Swift forces you to convert one side. Choose conversion based on intent: converting an Int to Double preserves the numeric value and precision for fractional math, while converting a Double to Int truncates the decimal portion and can lose information. Another subtle point is operator behavior: division of Int values uses integer division semantics so you might not get a fractional result when expected. If you expect fractions, ensure you operate with Doubles. Concrete example: calculating a player's hit accuracy as hits divided by total attempts — use Double to represent the ratio rather than Int to avoid truncation. Finally, remember that type annotation clarifies intent when inference might pick an unexpected type from a literal.

keyIdea.text: Use Int for exact whole values and Double when decimals matter; convert explicitly when combining them to avoid type errors or unintended truncation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Int vs Double
Int (whole numbers)
Use when values are counts or indices. Integer division truncates decimals.
Example
let lives: Int = 3 // whole number of lives
Double (decimal numbers)
Use when precision or fractions matter. Good for ratios, averages, version numbers.
Example
let accuracy: Double = 0.75 // 75% accuracy
Conversion example
let hits: Int = 75
let attempts: Int = 100
// Convert to Double for accurate ratio
let accuracy: Double = Double(hits) / Double(attempts) // 0.75
Misconception: dividing two Ints will give fractional expectations. Convert to Double when you want the fractional result.

screens.title: String Interpolation and Safe Display
screens.narratorSegment: String interpolation is Swift’s idiomatic way to build text that includes values. Instead of concatenating strings with plus signs, put the value inside the string using backslash parentheses. This keeps messages readable and prevents many type errors because interpolation converts values to text for display. For example, to show a player name and score you would write a single string that contains both values. One practice tip is to avoid creating long concatenation chains; interpolation expresses intent more clearly. Another practical point: interpolation can include expressions, not just variables, so you can format values or combine them inline. A common beginner mistake is trying to add an Int and a String directly; string interpolation avoids that by explicitly turning values into text within the literal. In Playgrounds, print the interpolated string to see how the values are substituted. Finally, interpolation helps with localization readiness because strings remain whole literals with placeholders rather than scattered concatenations. Try a short experiment: declare a player name and score, then print an interpolated sentence that summarizes the state. Notice how readable and safe the result is.

keyIdea.title: Interpolation tip
keyIdea.text: Use \(value) inside string literals to embed variables and expressions; it is clearer and safer than concatenation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › String Interpolation
Why interpolation
  • Makes messages readable and concise.
  • Avoids type-mismatch attempts to add strings and numbers.
  • Allows expressions inside the string for inline computation.
Code example
let playerName: String = "Alex"
let score: Int = 150
let message = "Player \(playerName) scored \(score) points!"
print(message) // Player Alex scored 150 points!
Pro tip: include expressions like \(score + bonus) to compute values inside the string at the point of formatting.

screens.title: Type Inference and Explicit Annotation
screens.narratorSegment: Swift’s type inference reduces clutter by deducing a value’s type from the initial value you assign. If you write var age = 30, Swift infers that age is an Int. If you write let price = 19.99, Swift infers a Double. This keeps code concise and often improves readability. However, there are times when explicit type annotation is helpful. Use annotation when the initial value alone does not express the desired type, when you want to document intent, or when you will assign a different but compatible value later. For example, declare var explicitAge: Int = 30 if you want to be explicit or if a literal could be interpreted multiple ways. One important misconception to avoid is assuming inference will always choose the type you need; sometimes numeric literals default to Double and later you may need an Int. Being deliberate with annotations avoids surprise conversions. Also, annotations help the compiler give clearer error messages because the intended type is explicit. Practice by declaring both inferred and annotated variables in a Playground and observe how the compiler displays their types and how it behaves when you mix types in expressions.

keyIdea.title: Inference vs annotation
keyIdea.text: Prefer inference for concise code, annotate when you need a specific type or clearer intent to avoid later conversion errors.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Inference & Annotation
Type Inference
Swift infers types from initial values so you often omit explicit types for brevity.
var temperature = 25.5 // inferred as Double
let greeting = "Good morning" // inferred as String
var isActive = true // inferred as Bool
When to annotate
Annotate when intent matters or inference is ambiguous, for example when numeric types could be Int or Double.
var explicitAge: Int = 30
let explicitPi: Double = 3.14159
Misconception

Inference always chooses the best type. In practice, inference follows simple rules and can pick Double for numeric literals; annotate when you need a different type.

screens.title: Basic Arithmetic and Operator Precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Arithmetic operations in Swift use the familiar operators: plus, minus, multiply, divide, and modulo for remainders. You can combine expressions, and Swift applies operator precedence so multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. This means expressions like 5 + 3 * 2 evaluate to eleven rather than sixteen. Use parentheses when you need a different order. When working with Int and Double, remember the type rules we covered: dividing two Int values performs integer division, which can truncate fractions, so convert to Double if you expect a fractional result. The modulo operator is useful for wrapping counters or checking even/odd status. A common beginner error is assuming division will produce a fractional result even when both operands are Int. Another practical tip: use compound assignment operators like += to update variables succinctly, for example incrementing a score. Practice by computing a total with bonuses and then printing the result using interpolation. This reinforces both arithmetic rules and type behavior in a single, practical example. Basic Arithmetic and Operator Precedence means use + - * / % for math, mind operator precedence, and convert types to avoid unexpected integer division or truncation.. In practical terms, perform numeric calculations and understand precedence rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Operators
  • + addition, - subtraction
  • * multiplication, / division
  • % remainder/modulo
Use parentheses to override precedence when needed.
Examples & tips
let total = 5 + 3 * 2 // 11 due to precedence
var score = 100
score += 50 // shorthand for score = score + 50
let remainder = 7 % 3 // 1
Convert Int to Double for fractional division: Double(a) / Double(b).

screens.title: Type Mismatch and Explicit Conversion
screens.narratorSegment: Swift’s type safety prevents many runtime surprises by disallowing operations between incompatible types. When you try to add a String and an Int, or a Double and an Int without conversion, the compiler raises an error. Instead of forcing implicit conversions, Swift requires you to convert explicitly so you make the intent clear. To fix a mismatch, convert values using initializers like Double(someInt) or String(someNumber). Choose the conversion direction that preserves the needed information. If you need precise fractional math, convert Int to Double before dividing. If you only need a display string, convert the number to String. A common mistake is to assume a conversion is lossless; converting Double to Int truncates the fraction. Another pitfall is over-converting everything; excessive conversions add noise. Practice converting only at the boundaries where different types must interact, and prefer keeping internal arithmetic within a single numeric type. This makes reasoning and debugging easier and keeps the compiler’s help aligned with your intent. Type Mismatch and Explicit Conversion means when types differ, convert explicitly using initializers and pick the direction that preserves the information you need.. In practical terms, how to resolve incompatible-type errors and preserve intent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: When types differ, convert explicitly using initializers and pick the direction that preserves the information you need.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Type Mismatch
Common error
Attempting operations across incompatible types causes compile-time errors. Swift wants explicit conversions so you choose the right behavior.
Example mistake
let name = "Alex"
let score = 150
// "Name: " + score   // ERROR: cannot add String and Int
Fix with conversion
let message = "Player \(name) scored \(score) points" // use interpolation
// or explicitly convert
let scoreText = String(score)
let message2 = "Player: " + scoreText
Choose conversion direction thoughtfully: converting Int to Double preserves fractions if you need fractional math; converting Double to Int truncates decimals.

import Foundation

// 1. Declare a constant for the maximum score
let maxScore: Int = 1000
print("Maximum possible score: \(maxScore)")

// 2. Declare a variable for the current score and update it
var currentScore: Int = 500
print("Initial score: \(currentScore)")
currentScore += 250
print("Score after bonus: \(currentScore)")

// 3. A value inferred as Double

print("Game version: \(gameVersion)")

// 4. A player's name (String)

// 5. A boolean value

print("Is game paused? \(isGamePaused)")

screens.title: Common Type-Related Errors and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: As you learn Swift, three error types will appear frequently: reassignment to a let constant, type mismatch between incompatible types, and unintended truncation when converting Double to Int. Reassignment errors happen when you try to change a value defined with let; the fix is straightforward — use var if you truly need mutability, or reconsider whether the value should change. Type mismatches occur when mixing Strings and numbers or Ints and Doubles; resolve them with explicit conversions or by using string interpolation for display. Unintended truncation happens when you convert a Double to an Int — the fractional part is lost. If you need approximate rounding, use rounding functions; if you need exact fractional math, keep values as Double. Another helpful habit is to read compiler messages carefully; they often suggest the exact conversion required. Lastly, avoid overusing conversions; keep numerical computation within a single numeric type until you reach the display or A P I boundary. This makes debugging easier and preserves numerical correctness. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Swift stores information and why those choices matter. We use named containers — variables and constants — to hold numbers, text, and true/false flags. Swift differentiates between mutable storage, declared with var, and immutable storage, declared with let. That distinction prevents accidental changes and makes reasoning about code easier. You will also meet the core types you use every day: Int for whole numbers, Double for decimals, String for text, and Bool for true/false values. Swift is type-safe and uses type inference to deduce types from initial values, while letting you add explicit type annotations when clarity or conversion is required. We will practice arithmetic operators and string interpolation to build readable output messages. Along the way, you’ll see common beginner mistakes — like trying to add strings and numbers without converting — and learn simple fixes. By the end of this chapter you will be able to declare variables and constants, pick appropriate types, use type inference with confidence, and produce formatted messages using interpolation. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you use every time you save or display data in an iOS app.

Over the next screens you will gain practical skills with Swift's core storage and types. First, you will learn how to choose between var and let by understanding mutability and why immutable values help prevent bugs. Second, you will identify Int, Double, String, and Bool, and be able to pick the right type for a value. Third, you will recognize how Swift infers types from initial values and when explicit annotation is useful for clarity or conversion. Fourth, you will perform arithmetic operations and use string interpolation to create clear output messages. Each objective ties directly to common tasks in an iOS app: keeping player scores, storing user names, tracking flags, and showing readable messages. You will practice in a Playground so you can see results immediately. As you work, notice how the compiler guides you; it’s not just syntax — it’s a safety net. By completing these objectives you will be ready to store and display data without common type mismatches and with clearer intent. A quick question to carry forward: when in doubt, ask whether a value will change during its lifetime.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and common pitfalls you'll encounter. You will run small experiments in a Swift Playground to declare constants and variables, update values, and immediately observe the results. The practice helps you internalize when a value should be let or var and how the compiler responds when you try to reassign an immutable value. You will also learn to spot type mismatches: attempting to combine a String and an Int without conversion, or assuming a Double can be used where an Int is expected. These are compile-time errors Swift uses to keep your code safe. Finally, you will learn simple fixes: explicit conversions such as wrapping an Int with Double(), or converting a number to a String for display. The hands-on routine mirrors real app work — keeping scores, showing versions, and printing summaries — so the skills transfer directly. A habit to form: run small changes and observe the Playground output; the immediate feedback helps you learn the language's rules quickly.

Start by treating var and let as the language’s way of saying whether a named container is allowed to change. A variable declared with var is mutable: you may reassign it later. For example, you might declare a player's current score with var because it updates during gameplay. A constant declared with let is immutable; once set, its value cannot be changed. The compiler enforces this by producing an error if you attempt reassignment. That enforcement is important: prefer let whenever a value does not need to change. Using let makes reasoning and refactoring easier because other code can rely on that value staying stable. A common misconception is that var is always safer for flexibility; in fact, overusing var leads to accidental state changes and bugs. A short example: declare let maxAttempts = 3 for a fixed rule and var currentAttempt = 0 for a counter. Try reassigning maxAttempts and the compiler flags the error — that immediate feedback prevents runtime surprises. Takeaway: decide on mutability at the moment of declaration. Ask yourself, will this value need to change? If not, use let. That simple rule leads to cleaner, more reliable code.

Understanding the four foundational types in this chapter helps you model everyday app data. Int stores whole numbers like lives, scores, and counts. Use Int when fractional values are not needed. Double stores floating-point numbers with decimals — for example, a version number or a measured value. String holds text such as user names, messages, or labels. Bool represents true/false conditions and is ideal for flags like whether a game is paused. Picking the appropriate type makes operations clear: arithmetic on numbers, concatenation or interpolation on strings, and conditional checks on booleans. A common beginner error is treating numbers as strings for display and then attempting arithmetic without converting them back. Another frequent confusion is when to prefer Double over Int; if you need fractions or precise decimal math, choose Double. Remember that Swift is type-safe, so mixing types requires explicit conversion. For instance, to add a Double and an Int you convert the Int into a Double, or convert the Double to an Int if you accept truncation. These choices affect correctness and clarity. Think of types as labels that tell both the compiler and future readers what kind of data is expected and how it should be used.

Deciding between Int and Double depends on whether fractional values are meaningful in your domain. Use Int for counts, indices, and values that should remain whole, like the number of lives or integer scores. Use Double for measurements, averages, or version numbers that can include decimals. A common pitfall is mixing these types without conversion. For example, adding a Double to an Int directly is not allowed; Swift forces you to convert one side. Choose conversion based on intent: converting an Int to Double preserves the numeric value and precision for fractional math, while converting a Double to Int truncates the decimal portion and can lose information. Another subtle point is operator behavior: division of Int values uses integer division semantics so you might not get a fractional result when expected. If you expect fractions, ensure you operate with Doubles. Concrete example: calculating a player's hit accuracy as hits divided by total attempts — use Double to represent the ratio rather than Int to avoid truncation. Finally, remember that type annotation clarifies intent when inference might pick an unexpected type from a literal.

String interpolation is Swift’s idiomatic way to build text that includes values. Instead of concatenating strings with plus signs, put the value inside the string using backslash parentheses. This keeps messages readable and prevents many type errors because interpolation converts values to text for display. For example, to show a player name and score you would write a single string that contains both values. One practice tip is to avoid creating long concatenation chains; interpolation expresses intent more clearly. Another practical point: interpolation can include expressions, not just variables, so you can format values or combine them inline. A common beginner mistake is trying to add an Int and a String directly; string interpolation avoids that by explicitly turning values into text within the literal. In Playgrounds, print the interpolated string to see how the values are substituted. Finally, interpolation helps with localization readiness because strings remain whole literals with placeholders rather than scattered concatenations. Try a short experiment: declare a player name and score, then print an interpolated sentence that summarizes the state. Notice how readable and safe the result is.

Swift’s type inference reduces clutter by deducing a value’s type from the initial value you assign. If you write var age = 30, Swift infers that age is an Int. If you write let price = 19.99, Swift infers a Double. This keeps code concise and often improves readability. However, there are times when explicit type annotation is helpful. Use annotation when the initial value alone does not express the desired type, when you want to document intent, or when you will assign a different but compatible value later. For example, declare var explicitAge: Int = 30 if you want to be explicit or if a literal could be interpreted multiple ways. One important misconception to avoid is assuming inference will always choose the type you need; sometimes numeric literals default to Double and later you may need an Int. Being deliberate with annotations avoids surprise conversions. Also, annotations help the compiler give clearer error messages because the intended type is explicit. Practice by declaring both inferred and annotated variables in a Playground and observe how the compiler displays their types and how it behaves when you mix types in expressions.

Arithmetic operations in Swift use the familiar operators: plus, minus, multiply, divide, and modulo for remainders. You can combine expressions, and Swift applies operator precedence so multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. This means expressions like 5 + 3 * 2 evaluate to eleven rather than sixteen. Use parentheses when you need a different order. When working with Int and Double, remember the type rules we covered: dividing two Int values performs integer division, which can truncate fractions, so convert to Double if you expect a fractional result. The modulo operator is useful for wrapping counters or checking even/odd status. A common beginner error is assuming division will produce a fractional result even when both operands are Int. Another practical tip: use compound assignment operators like += to update variables succinctly, for example incrementing a score. Practice by computing a total with bonuses and then printing the result using interpolation. This reinforces both arithmetic rules and type behavior in a single, practical example.
